Why Belong to a Faith Community?

Read, reflect, and take the time you need.

Section 1 of 12

If religious institutions have hurt people, why join one?

The word “church” can bring different feelings.

For some, it brings memories of family, music, friendship, and prayer. For others, it brings distrust, judgment, control, hypocrisy, or abuse.

Many Native people have good reasons to be cautious. Churches were involved in boarding schools, forced religious instruction, punishment for speaking Native languages, and attempts to replace Native identity with European culture.

Those wrongs should not be minimized or defended.

Jesus never gave religious institutions permission to abuse people, hide wrongdoing, or erase their identity. When churches acted that way, they misrepresented Him.

So why would Jesus still invite us into a faith community?

Because the church, as Jesus designed it, is not a building, political power, or culture-changing institution. It is a family of people who follow Him, learn His Word, care for one another, and carry His message to the world.

Jesus created a community, not just isolated followers

Read Matthew 16:13–18 ↗.

Jesus said, “I will build My church.”

The Bible uses the word “church” to describe people who have been called together. A church may meet in a large building, a small home, a rented room, or online when distance makes gathering difficult.

The people—not the building—are the church.

When Jesus called His first disciples, He did not ask them to follow Him alone. He formed a community. They traveled together, learned together, served together, disagreed, forgave one another, and grew.

A personal relationship with Jesus is essential, but the Bible does not describe spiritual life as a permanently isolated journey.

We need one another

Read Hebrews 10:24–25 ↗.

The Bible tells believers to gather, encourage one another, and help one another grow in love and good works.

Life can be heavy. There will be days when your faith feels strong and days when you struggle to pray. A healthy faith community gives you people who can:

  • Pray with you
  • Help you understand the Bible
  • Encourage you when you feel discouraged
  • Correct you with patience when you are moving in a harmful direction
  • Bring practical help during sickness or crisis
  • Celebrate answered prayers with you
  • Give you opportunities to serve

Watching a service online can be helpful, especially if you live far from a healthy congregation. But a livestream cannot fully replace being known, supported, and given a place to use your gifts.

We were created for connection.

Every person has something to contribute

Read 1 Corinthians 12:12–27 ↗.

The Bible compares the community of Jesus to a human body. A body has many parts, and every part has a purpose.

You may think you have nothing important to offer. You may not preach, sing, or lead publicly. But the Holy Spirit gives every believer abilities that can strengthen others.

Your gift might be:

  • Listening without judging
  • Encouraging young people
  • Helping families
  • Teaching the Bible clearly
  • Preparing food
  • Repairing things
  • Organizing projects
  • Praying faithfully
  • Creating music or art
  • Showing hospitality
  • Caring for elders
  • Helping people who are struggling financially

You were not created merely to attend, watch, and leave. You have something your spiritual community needs.

Baptism welcomes you into a spiritual family

Read Acts 2:38–47 ↗.

People who accepted Jesus were baptized and added to the community of believers. They learned together, prayed, shared meals, worshiped, and helped people in need.

Baptism is a commitment to Jesus, but it also connects you with His people.

Church membership should not mean surrendering control of your mind or allowing leaders to own your conscience. It is a covenant to worship, learn, serve, and grow with other believers.

Jesus remains the head of the church. Read Colossians 1:18 ↗.

Pastors, teachers, and elders are servants. They do not stand between you and the Creator, and they do not have authority to contradict the Bible.

Not every congregation represents Jesus well

A building may have the word “church” on its sign and still fail to follow Jesus.

Some congregations teach human traditions above the Bible. Some protect powerful leaders instead of protecting people. Some are more interested in money, politics, appearance, or control than in truth and love.

Jesus warned that false teachers would come in His name. Read Matthew 7:15–23 ↗.

That means you should not join a congregation simply because:

  • Your family has always attended it
  • The speaker is entertaining
  • The music creates strong feelings
  • The building is impressive
  • The group is popular online
  • A leader claims special authority
  • People pressure you to decide quickly

The Creator invites you to examine what a congregation teaches and how it treats people.

How can you recognize a faithful congregation?

No congregation is perfect, because every congregation is made of imperfect people. But the Bible gives clear signs to look for.

It places the Bible above human tradition

Read Isaiah 8:20 ↗ and Acts 17:11 ↗.

A faithful congregation welcomes sincere questions and encourages people to read Scripture for themselves.

Its leaders do not say, “Do not question us.” They say, “Examine the Bible and see whether what we teach is true.”

It makes Jesus central

Read John 5:39 ↗ and Acts 4:12 ↗.

A faithful congregation teaches that salvation comes through Jesus—not through membership, ancestry, ceremonies, money, or human achievement.

Jesus is honored as Creator, Savior, High Priest, returning King, and Head of the church.

It teaches salvation by grace

Read Ephesians 2:8–10 ↗.

We cannot earn salvation through obedience or good behavior. We are saved by grace through faith.

Grace does not make obedience unnecessary. It changes the heart so that we want to follow the Creator.

It honors all Ten Commandments

Read John 14:15 ↗ and Revelation 14:12 ↗.

A faithful congregation does not remove the commandments that have become unpopular. It teaches love for the Creator and love for people, including the seventh-day Sabbath.

It teaches the complete message of Scripture

A faithful congregation does not build its entire message around one favorite teaching.

It helps people understand:

  • Creation
  • The life, death, and resurrection of Jesus
  • Salvation by grace
  • The work of the Holy Spirit
  • The Ten Commandments
  • The seventh-day Sabbath
  • Baptism by immersion
  • What happens when people die
  • The heavenly judgment
  • The visible return of Jesus
  • The resurrection
  • Healthy living
  • Stewardship
  • The final conflict between truth and deception

The Bible is allowed to correct personal opinions and religious traditions.

It prepares people for the return of Jesus

Read Revelation 14:6–12 ↗.

Revelation describes a worldwide message for every nation, tribe, language, and people.

This message announces the everlasting gospel, calls people to worship the Creator, warns against spiritual confusion, and identifies those who remain faithful to Jesus and His commandments.

A faithful congregation does more than help people feel comfortable. It lovingly prepares them for what is coming.

It demonstrates the character of Jesus

Read John 13:34–35 ↗ and Galatians 5:22–23 ↗.

Correct teachings matter, but correct teachings without love can become another form of religious harm.

A congregation that represents Jesus should grow in:

  • Love
  • Joy
  • Peace
  • Patience
  • Kindness
  • Goodness
  • Faithfulness
  • Gentleness
  • Self-control

People should be treated with dignity. Children and vulnerable adults should be protected. Abuse should never be hidden to preserve a leader’s reputation.

Forgiveness does not remove accountability. Serious wrongdoing should be addressed honestly, and people in danger should be helped to find safety.

It respects people from every nation

Read Revelation 7:9–10 ↗.

The Creator’s family includes people from every nation, tribe, and language. Unity in Jesus does not require cultural sameness.

A healthy congregation will not demand that you:

  • Become culturally white
  • Feel ashamed of being Native
  • Reject your family name or language
  • Pretend historical harm never happened
  • Accept stereotypes about your people
  • Allow your identity to be used as decoration or marketing

It should listen before making assumptions. If a particular belief or practice conflicts with the Bible, the concern should be explained carefully and specifically. An entire people or culture should never be carelessly condemned.

Does the Creator have faithful people in other churches?

Read John 10:16 ↗.

Jesus said He has sheep who are not yet gathered into one fold.

The Creator has sincere people in many congregations. Some follow Jesus faithfully according to the truth they currently understand. We should not act as though everyone outside our congregation is dishonest or rejected by God.

At the same time, sincerity does not make every teaching correct.

Read Revelation 18:1–4 ↗.

The Creator calls His people out of spiritual confusion and into greater truth. That invitation is an act of love, not condemnation.

The question is not, “Are there kind people in this congregation?”

The deeper question is, “Does this congregation faithfully follow the complete message of the Bible?”

Revelation describes a faithful final community

Read Revelation 12:17 ↗.

Revelation describes a people against whom the dragon is angry. They are identified by two qualities:

  1. They keep the commandments of God.
  2. They have the testimony of Jesus.

Revelation 19:10 ↗ connects the testimony of Jesus with the Spirit of prophecy. A faithful final community will respect the Holy Spirit’s prophetic work while testing every message by Scripture.

This community does not earn salvation by keeping commandments. Its members obey because they trust and love Jesus.

The word “remnant” describes those who remain faithful when truth is unpopular. It is not a title people should use to boast that they are better than everyone else.

If a congregation claims to be faithful but is proud, controlling, dishonest, or cruel, its behavior contradicts its claim.

Truth should produce humility.

Warning signs of an unhealthy congregation

Be cautious if a congregation or leader:

  • Claims to be above questions
  • Uses fear to control decisions
  • Pressures you for money
  • Demands unquestioning loyalty to a person
  • Tells you to ignore clear Bible teaching
  • Covers up abuse or protects offenders
  • Tries to isolate you from safe family and friends
  • Treats women, children, elders, or outsiders without dignity
  • Makes political loyalty a test of faith
  • Treats your culture as entirely evil
  • Uses Native images or language without meaningful Native relationships
  • Pushes you toward baptism or membership before you understand the commitment

Healthy spiritual leadership does not fear accountability.

If you see serious warning signs, seek wise help. You are not betraying Jesus by refusing manipulation or abuse.

What if you have been hurt by a church?

You do not need to pretend the harm did not happen.

You may need time to heal. You may need help from a counselor, trusted elder, mature believer, or another safe person. You may need strong boundaries with those who harmed you.

Forgiveness and restored trust are not the same thing. Forgiveness can begin in your heart, but trust must be rebuilt through honesty, repentance, and changed behavior.

Do not let an abusive institution define Jesus for you.

Read Matthew 11:28–30 ↗.

Jesus is gentle with wounded people. He does not shame you for being careful. Ask Him to guide you toward people who reflect His character.

How should you choose a congregation?

Take your time and pay attention.

Read its teachings

Ask what the congregation believes about Jesus, salvation, the Bible, the Sabbath, death, prophecy, baptism, and the Second Coming.

Attend more than once

One service may not reveal the character of a community. Observe how people treat one another over time.

Ask questions

A healthy leader will not become angry because you want biblical answers.

Speak with members

Ask whether leaders are accountable, how concerns are handled, and whether people are encouraged to think and study.

Watch how vulnerable people are treated

Notice how the congregation treats children, elders, people with disabilities, struggling families, and those without money or influence.

Pray for guidance

Ask the Creator to lead you through His Word and the Holy Spirit—not merely through feelings or pressure.

You do not have to lose yourself to belong

Jesus is building a family from every nation. He is not turning every nation into one human culture.

You can bring your voice, experiences, abilities, and story into His community. You can help others understand concerns they may never have considered.

Your presence should not be treated as a diversity symbol. You are a full member of the body of Jesus, with gifts, responsibilities, and a voice that matters.

Belonging to Jesus connects you with people beyond your nation without separating you from your people.

Think About It

  1. What feelings come to mind when you hear the word “church”?
  2. Have religious people helped you, hurt you, or both?
  3. Why does Jesus call believers into community instead of asking everyone to follow Him alone?
  4. Which signs of a healthy congregation matter most to you?
  5. What warning signs should you take seriously?
  6. What gifts or experiences could you contribute to a faith community?

Try This During the Coming Week

Day 1

Read Matthew 16:13–18 ↗.

Write down what this passage teaches about Jesus and His church.

Day 2

Read Acts 2:38–47 ↗.

List what the early community did together.

Day 3

Read 1 Corinthians 12:12–27 ↗.

Ask the Creator to show you what gifts you could use to help others.

Day 4

Read Acts 17:10–12 ↗.

Choose one teaching you have heard and compare it carefully with the Bible.

Day 5

Read Revelation 12:17 ↗ and Revelation 14:6–12 ↗.

Write down the identifying marks of the Creator’s faithful final people.

Day 6

Read John 13:34–35 ↗ and Galatians 5:22–23 ↗.

Consider whether the religious communities you know display the character of Jesus.

Day 7

Visit or contact a seventh-day Sabbath-keeping congregation. Ask about its beliefs, community life, and opportunities to learn without pressure.

Afterward, pray about what you observed.

A Prayer You Can Pray

Creator, You know my experiences with religious people and institutions. Thank You for the good I have received, and please heal the wounds that remain.

Jesus, lead me to a community that follows Your Word and reflects Your character. Protect me from deception, control, pride, and abuse.

Give me wisdom to recognize truth. Help me ask honest questions and examine every teaching by the Bible.

Show me the gifts You have placed in my life and how I can use them to help others.

Please give me a spiritual family that respects my identity, honors my people, and places loyalty to You above every human tradition.

Help me belong without losing who You created me to be. Amen.

Remember This

The church is not merely a building or institution. It is a community of people called to follow Jesus together.

A faithful congregation places the Bible above tradition, makes Jesus central, teaches salvation by grace, honors all Ten Commandments, prepares people for His return, protects the vulnerable, and welcomes people from every nation.

Jesus does not ask you to surrender your Native identity to join His family.

He invites you to bring your whole life under His leadership and use your gifts to strengthen others.
